stimulus.text:
| Society | Environment | Main way of getting food | Settlement |
| Pueblo peoples | Arid Southwest | Dry farming of maize, beans, and squash | Permanent adobe villages |
| Iroquois villagers | Northeast woodlands | Three sisters farming, with hunting and fishing | Permanent villages |
| Chinook peoples | Rainy Pacific coast | Fishing, hunting, and foraging | Permanent villages with marked social ranks |
| Great Plains peoples | Grasslands | Bison hunting on foot, with some farming in river valleys | Mobile camps for much of the year |
| Great Basin peoples | Arid basin between mountain ranges | Hunting and gathering, moving with the seasons | Mobile camps |
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.

stem: Pueblo peoples farmed in the arid Southwest, Iroquois villagers lived in the woodlands of the Northeast, and the peoples of the Pacific Northwest built their lives around fishing. Taken together, what do these examples best illustrate?

options.text: Native societies in every environment adopted identical farming methods and crops.
options.misconception: Reads different adaptations as identical methods.

options.text: Native societies shaped their economies and ways of life around their environments.
Only maize-farming societies ever established permanent settlements anywhere in the Americas.
options.misconception: Denies the settled fishing villages of the Pacific Northwest.

options.text: Geographic differences kept all Native societies completely isolated from one another.
options.misconception: Turns different environments into total isolation.

rationales.A: The examples show different adaptations, not identical farming methods and crops.
rationales.B: Dry farming, woodland village farming, and coastal fishing each fit a particular environment.
rationales.C: Pacific Northwest fishing peoples maintained settled villages without maize agriculture.
rationales.D: The table shows different adaptations, not societies cut off from one another.
rationales.general:
1. List the three cases. Pueblo farmers in the dry Southwest, Iroquois villagers in the Northeast woodlands, and fishing peoples on the Pacific coast.
2. Compare the work. Farming, village life, and fishing are three different ways of living.
3. Ask what differs. The land differs, so the way of life differs with it: the land wrote the menu, and each people ate what it offered.
4. Name the pattern. Each society shaped its economy around its own environment.
Remember: when cases differ together, look for the condition that differs with them.
